question: In the Navigation Rules, what is a "stand-on vessel" required to do when meeting another vessel?
choice_a: Always stop dead in the water immediately
choice_b: Maintain its course and speed, unless a collision becomes imminent, in which case it must take whatever action best avoids the collision
choice_c: Immediately turn hard to starboard regardless of the situation
choice_d: Sound five short blasts and reverse engines
explanation: The Connecticut Boater's Guide defines the stand-on vessel as the one that should maintain its course and speed unless collision becomes imminent, at which point it must act to avoid the collision.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Terms to Know," p.34

question: What must a "give-way vessel" do under the Navigation Rules when it is required to yield to another vessel?
choice_a: Speed up to clear the other vessel's path as quickly as possible
choice_b: Wait until the last possible moment to react
choice_c: Take early and substantial action to avoid collision, such as stopping, slowing down, or changing course
choice_d: Do nothing and rely on the other vessel to move
explanation: A give-way vessel must take early and substantial action -- stopping, slowing, or changing course -- to keep well clear of the vessel it must yield to, rather than waiting until a collision is imminent.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Terms to Know," p.34

question: Under the sound signals used on Connecticut and U.S. waters when vessels are within half a mile of each other and in sight of one another, what does one short blast mean?
choice_d: "I intend to leave you on my port side"
explanation: Among the four sound signals recognized in Connecticut for vessels in sight of each other, one short blast signals "I intend to leave you on my port side," two short blasts signal starboard side, three short blasts signal operating astern propulsion, and five or more blasts signal danger or disagreement.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Sound Signals," p.33

question: What do five or more short blasts mean when signaled by a vessel on Connecticut or U.S. waters?
choice_a: It indicates danger or that the signaling vessel does not understand or agree with the other vessel's intentions
choice_b: It signals that the vessel is anchoring for the night
choice_c: It means the vessel is requesting a fuel refill
choice_d: It has no defined meaning under the Navigation Rules
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger signal under the Navigation Rules, used when a vessel does not understand the other's intentions or believes insufficient action is being taken to avoid collision.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Sound Signals," p.33

question: When a high-speed ferry (HSF) capable of 60 knots (about 70 mph) or more is approaching on Long Island Sound, what should a recreational boater do?
choice_a: Ignore it since ferries always have to yield to recreational boats
choice_b: Know and obey the USCG rules of the road, make any course or speed changes early and obviously while still at least one mile from the HSF, and monitor VHF Channel 13 for its announcements
choice_c: Cut directly across its bow to save time
choice_d: Turn off all navigation lights so it can see you better
explanation: Because high-speed ferries operating on Long Island Sound can approach very quickly, Connecticut's Boater's Guide instructs recreational boaters to obey the rules of the road, make early and obvious maneuvers while still a mile away, monitor VHF Channel 13, and display proper running lights and a radar reflector at night or in reduced visibility.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "High Speed Ferries," p.33

question: Under the general prudential rule that underlies the Navigation Rules, what is every operator responsible for regardless of stand-on or give-way status?
choice_a: Only watching for other boats larger than their own
choice_b: Assuming other vessels will always follow the rules perfectly
choice_c: Maintaining a proper lookout and taking whatever action is necessary to avoid a collision, even if it departs from the normal rules
choice_d: Nothing -- once designated stand-on, no action is ever required
explanation: The general prudential rule requires every operator to keep a proper lookout and take whatever action is necessary to avoid collision, even departing from the normal navigation rules if the immediate danger of collision requires it -- a universal safety principle underlying all Navigation Rules.
source_note: General Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 2, Rule of Good Seamanship), universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: Under the Navigation Rules' priority hierarchy, which type of vessel generally has the right-of-way over a sailing vessel operating under sail alone?
choice_c: No vessel type ever outranks a sailing vessel under sail
choice_d: A vessel not under command or one restricted in its ability to maneuver
explanation: The general right-of-way hierarchy places vessels not under command and vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver above sailing vessels, which in turn generally outrank ordinary power-driven vessels; this order exists because less maneuverable vessels need the most protection from vessels able to more easily change course or speed.
source_note: General Navigation Rules right-of-way hierarchy, universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: In a head-on meeting situation between two power-driven vessels, what is the standard rule for passing?
choice_a: Each vessel should alter course to starboard so they pass port side to port side
choice_b: Both vessels should stop and wait for instructions from shore
choice_c: The larger vessel always has right-of-way regardless of position
choice_d: Each vessel should turn to port to pass starboard to starboard
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the standard rule is for each power-driven vessel to alter course to starboard, resulting in the vessels passing each other port side to port side, similar to cars driving on the right.
source_note: General Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 14, head-on situations), universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: Under the Navigation Rules, which vessel in an overtaking situation must keep clear of the other, regardless of whether the overtaking vessel is under sail or power?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken must always get out of the way
choice_b: The overtaking vessel must always keep clear of the vessel being overtaken, until it is finally past and clear
choice_c: Whichever vessel is faster automatically has the right-of-way
choice_d: Overtaking situations are not addressed by the Navigation Rules
explanation: In an overtaking situation, the vessel doing the overtaking is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken until it is finally past and clear, regardless of the propulsion type of either vessel.
source_note: General Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 13, overtaking), universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What must every vessel do under crowded conditions or in reduced visibility, according to Connecticut's Boater's Guide?
choice_a: Speed up to clear the area faster
choice_b: Turn off all lights to avoid confusing other boaters
choice_c: Slow down and operate with careful regard for the existing circumstances and conditions
choice_d: Nothing different is required regardless of visibility
explanation: The Boater's Guide requires every vessel, under crowded conditions or in reduced visibility, to slow down and operate with careful regard for existing circumstances -- speeding in confined areas under these conditions can be treated as reckless or negligent operation.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Restricted Operating Distances and Speed Regulations," p.24

question: What is a narrow channel, and what rule generally applies to vessels using one under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: A channel that only sailboats may use
choice_b: A waterway where any vessel may travel on whichever side it prefers with no guidance
choice_c: A channel where speed limits never apply
choice_d: A restricted waterway where vessels should keep as far to the starboard (right) side as safe and practicable, similar to a traffic lane
explanation: In a narrow channel or fairway, a vessel should keep to the starboard side of the channel where it is safe and practicable to do so, similar to staying in the proper lane on a road, and a vessel under 20 meters or a sailing vessel generally should not impede a vessel that can only navigate safely within the channel.
source_note: General Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 9, narrow channels), universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum
